# GitHub key for agents

The GitHub key is stored in the macOS login keychain. Agents on this Mac fetch it when they need it, so it never has to sit in a plaintext file.

## Where things are

| Item | Location |
|---|---|
| Key | Login keychain, service `github-api-key`, account = your macOS user |
| Print the key | `/Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-token` |
| Git credential helper | `/Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-git-credential` |
| Git setting | `~/.gitconfig`, key `credential.https://github.com.helper` |
| Agent instructions | `.claude-home/CLAUDE.md` and `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (Claude Code), `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` (Codex), `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` and `~/.gemini/AGENTS.md` (Antigravity), `~/.hermes/SOUL.md` (Hermes), `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` (OpenCode) |

## How to use it

Run a command with the key in an environment variable. The value is set for that one command and never saved:

```bash
GITHUB_TOKEN="$(/Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-token)" <command>
```

Call the GitHub REST API with curl. The `gh` CLI isn't installed.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $(/Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-token)" -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" https://api.github.com/user
```

Use git over HTTPS as usual. The credential helper supplies the key, so remote URLs stay plain:

```bash
git push
```

The key isn't exported from `~/.zshrc`, so it isn't in every process's environment. Use the inline pattern above.

Rules for agents and people using this key:

- Never print the key, write it to a file, paste it into chat, or commit it.
- Don't copy the key from any file. Get it from the helper.
- Ask first before deleting repos, packages or releases, or changing org or repo settings.
- If something fails, report the error. Don't search for another token.

## Scope of the key

It's a classic token for `alexanderh2seo4`, with broad scopes that include `repo`, `workflow`, `delete_repo`, `admin:org` and `admin:enterprise`. To see the full list:

```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - -H "Authorization: Bearer $(/Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-token)" https://api.github.com/user | grep -i '^x-oauth-scopes'
```

Classic tokens can't be limited to specific repos. A fine-grained token can, and it's the safer choice for agents. See [Replace the key](#replace-the-key).

## Test it

Run the tests in order. Each one has an expected result.

| # | Test | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Helper prints the key | `41` (the 40-character key plus a newline) |
| 2 | GitHub accepts the key | `alexanderh2seo4` |
| 3 | git can reach GitHub | `git auth ok` |
| 4 | git helper answers | Output includes `username=x-access-token` and `password=<redacted>` |
| 5 | Codex runs the helper | `41` |
| 6 | Codex reaches GitHub | `alexanderh2seo4` |

**Test 1**

```bash
/Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-token | wc -c
```

**Test 2**

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $(/Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-token)" https://api.github.com/user | jq -r .login
```

**Test 3**

```bash
GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 git ls-remote --heads https://github.com/alexanderh2seo4/SSH-acces.git > /dev/null && echo "git auth ok"
```

**Test 4** (the password is redacted in the output)

```bash
printf 'protocol=https\nhost=github.com\n\n' | git credential fill | sed -E 's/^(password=).*/\1<redacted>/'
```

**Tests 5 and 6 in Codex**

Start Codex in this folder and paste this prompt for test 5:

> Run `/Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-token | wc -c` and reply with only the number.

Expected: `41`. Then paste this prompt for test 6:

> Run `curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $(/Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-token)" https://api.github.com/user | jq -r .login` and reply with only the output.

Expected: `alexanderh2seo4`.

To run both checks from Terminal instead, first `cd` into this folder. Test 5:

```bash
codex exec --skip-git-repo-check "Run this exact shell command and reply with only its output: /Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-token | wc -c"
```

Test 6:

```bash
codex exec --skip-git-repo-check "Run this exact shell command and reply with only its output: curl -s -H \"Authorization: Bearer \$(/Users/alexanderkluge/.local/bin/github-token)\" https://api.github.com/user | jq -r .login"
```

The last line of each output should be the expected value.

## If something fails

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Test 1 prints `0` | The login keychain is locked | Run `security unlock-keychain ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db` and enter your Mac password |
| `The specified item could not be found` | The keychain item is missing | Replace the key (below) |
| Test 2 prints `Bad credentials` | The token was revoked or has expired | Replace the key (below) |
| Test 3 fails or asks for a username | The git helper isn't registered | `git config --global --get-all credential.https://github.com.helper` should print an empty line and the helper path |
| Codex reports a keychain or network error | The Codex sandbox blocked it | Report the error. Don't work around the sandbox |

## Replace the key

Run this in your own Terminal, not in Codex. It asks for the new token with hidden input:

```bash
security add-generic-password -U -s github-api-key -a "$(id -un)" -w
```

Then run tests 1 and 2 again. Once they pass, revoke the old token at https://github.com/settings/tokens.

# AGENTS.md — read this first

## What we're building

**ReqFlow** is a hackathon prototype for the BMW challenge _"AI for Product Decision Making"_: a
**native desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux** (Electron, not a web app) with three tabs. On
**Data Flow**, an n8n-style flow of **building blocks** (Custom, Raw, Research, AI Filter, AI Splitter,
HIL, Add to Car; some expand into their own inner workplace) turns customer and market data into
prioritized, evidence-linked car requirements. The **Car** tab shows them for the PM to review, and
**Settings** configures the app, global parameters and collaboration. Full spec: [PRODUCT.md](PRODUCT.md). Your task: [docs/WORKSTREAMS.md](docs/WORKSTREAMS.md).
Current state and handoffs: [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md).

## The challenge in brief (from `context/`)

- **Goal:** help BMW product managers define, justify and prioritize **customer-facing requirements
  for the successor** of an existing vehicle, thinking **3–5 years ahead**. The PM stays in control of
  every decision.
- **Vehicles and markets:** the 1, 5 or 7 Series, in Europe, China or the US. Demo **one derivative in one
  market** (ours: 1 Series F70, EU), but don't build a one-off.
- **BMW provides, per vehicle:** customer feedback, equipment data, sales volumes and a customer study.
  We may add web sources such as competitors, reviews and market or technology trends.
- **The app must:** ingest the data and enrich it from the web → extract signals (complaints, unmet needs,
  competitor advantages, trends), **each linked to its sources** → derive clear, actionable, realistic
  requirements → prioritize them with explainable logic → let the PM approve, reject, edit or challenge
  them → record everything in an **audit trail** (who or what, when, and why).
- **Each requirement needs:** a unique ID, an actionable description, linked findings and sources, a
  priority or score, the prioritization rationale, an evidence level, assumptions and uncertainties, and
  a decision status.
- **In scope:** features, equipment, comfort, space, usability, infotainment and digital services,
  design and quality perception, driving experience, range and charging as the customer experiences them,
  and variants and packages. **Out of scope:** regulatory and homologation topics, engineering specs, and
  pricing or business cases (rough effort may be used as a priority factor).
- **Judges value:** trustworthy sources, transparent reasoning, thoughtful prioritization, honest
  handling of uncertainty and **conflicting evidence**, and focus on customer value. Depth in one area
  beats shallow coverage of everything.
- **BMW process we mirror:** situation analysis → structure and context (classify, cluster, dedupe) →
  requirements definition (measurable targets and acceptance criteria) → prioritization (customer and
  business) → documentation and tracking. _"From 1 billion findings to 1,000 requirements to one car."_

## Rules for every agent

1. **Stay in your lane.** Edit only the paths your workstream owns (see WORKSTREAMS.md). Do you need
   something changed elsewhere? Write it in your final report instead of editing it yourself.
2. **`packages/core` is the contract.** Build against it and don't change it on your own. If you need a
   contract change, propose it in your final report. The lead merges contract changes.
3. **No real data in git, logs or transcripts.** BMW files go in `data/raw/` (gitignored). Entire
   publishes session transcripts, so when you inspect them, print only structure and counts (sheet
   and column names, row counts), never cell values, and never send them to delegated agents.
   Committed tests use synthetic data (`@reqflow/core/fixtures`, `data/samples/`). Never commit or
   print API keys.
4. **No silent failures.** Validate inputs with the Zod schemas, throw clear errors, and never invent
   sources or evidence. Every finding needs a verbatim excerpt.
5. **AI never decides.** Only a human sets `approved`, `rejected` or `deferred`. Every change to a
   requirement writes an AuditEvent.
6. **Prove it works.** Add colocated `*.test.ts` files. Before you report done, run
   `npm run typecheck && npm test` from the repo root. For UI work, also run `npm run smoke` and look at
   the screenshots in `apps/desktop/out/smoke/`.
7. **Respect the process split.** UI code (renderer) has no Node, no `fs` and no network. It talks to the
   main process only through `api` from `@/lib/api` (contract: `packages/core/src/ipc.ts`). Data, AI
   calls, files and API keys live in the main process. Build paths with `node:path` so they work on Windows.
8. **Sessions are tracked with [Entire](https://github.com/entireio/cli).** Commit with plain `git`.
   Entire attaches your session to each commit as a checkpoint and pushes it on `git push`. Don't
   remove its hooks (`.claude/settings.json`, `.git/hooks`) and never put secrets in prompts.

9. **Hand off in [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md).** Claim your workstream there when you start; your
   tasks are the checklist in its section, in priority order. Update your own section (and only that
   one) when you finish a slice, get blocked or stop: tick done tasks, add a log entry. The next agent
   starts from it. The repo and Entire transcripts are **public**, so never paste keys or BMW data anywhere.

## Commands (repo root, Node ≥ 22.13; works on Windows, macOS, Linux)

```
npm install          # once
npm run dev          # opens the desktop app with hot reload
npm run smoke        # builds, screenshots every screen, checks the IPC bridge
npm test             # vitest, all packages
npm run typecheck    # all workspaces
npm run format       # prettier
npm run package      # installer for your OS → apps/desktop/release/
```

```bash
entire enable --agent claude-code
```


# Architecture

ReqFlow is a **native desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux** (Electron), not a web app.
Background and alternatives: [decisions/0002-electron-desktop-app.md](decisions/0002-electron-desktop-app.md).
Why the flow is built from blocks: [decisions/0003-building-blocks.md](decisions/0003-building-blocks.md).

## Stack

| Concern         | Choice                                                                                | Why                                                                                                          |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Language        | TypeScript everywhere (npm workspaces)                                                | One shared contract for UI, engine and blocks                                                                |
| App shell       | Electron 44 (pinned, Node 24 inside), electron-vite 5, electron-builder               | Same Chromium on every OS; Node in the main process runs the engine                                          |
| UI              | React 19 + React Router (hash routing) + Tailwind 4 + zustand 5                       | Renders from `file://` in the installed app; small, testable stores                                          |
| Workflow canvas | `@xyflow/react` (React Flow 12)                                                       | The standard n8n-style node editor                                                                           |
| Schemas         | Zod 4                                                                                 | Runtime validation and TS types from one source                                                              |
| LLM             | Anthropic API and standalone Mastra Agent behind `LlmClient`, plus `mock`             | Swappable; works offline and in tests; Mastra is constructed per request without an attached Mastra instance |
| Persistence     | SQLite via built-in `node:sqlite`, in the OS app-data folder                          | Zero setup, no native module to rebuild per OS                                                               |
| Tests           | Vitest (colocated `*.test.ts`) + `npm run smoke` (clicks through the app in Electron) | Fast unit tests; a real-app check without clicking                                                           |

## Repo layout

```
.
├── AGENTS.md  PRODUCT.md  README.md   ← start here
├── context/                           ← original hackathon briefing + the app sketch (read-only)
├── docs/                              ← ARCHITECTURE, WORKSTREAMS, STATUS, decisions/ (ADRs)
├── data/
│   ├── raw/        (gitignored)       ← BMW-provided datasets
│   └── samples/                       ← small synthetic datasets for dev
├── packages/
│   ├── core/       ← CONTRACT: domain schemas, blocks.ts (block specs), graph.ts (graph rules), IPC API, fixtures
│   ├── engine/     ← block contract + registry (done); executor (WS1)
│   ├── blocks/     ← block implementations, one folder per block + default template
│   ├── llm/        ← LlmClient implementations: anthropic, mock (WS7)
│   └── db/         ← SQLite repositories, AuditLogger, FileStore (WS1)
└── apps/desktop/                      ← the Electron app
    ├── electron.vite.config.ts  electron-builder.yml  build/ (icons)
    └── src/
        ├── main/       ← Node: window, IPC handlers, wiring of engine/db/llm, smoke test
        ├── preload/    ← the bridge: allow-listed invoke + run-update events (keep tiny)
        └── renderer/src/
            ├── pages/        DataflowPage · CarPage · SettingsPage
            ├── components/   dataflow/ (editor + its store) · settings/ · shell/ (bottom tabs) · ui/ (shared controls)
            ├── lib/          api.ts (the only way to main) · settings.ts (settings store) · theme.ts
            └── router.tsx  globals.css (design tokens, light + dark)
```

Dependency direction (no cycles): `core ← engine ← blocks`, `core ← llm`, `core ← db`, and
`apps/desktop/src/main` → all of them. The renderer imports only `@reqflow/core` (types, block specs,
graph rules, fixtures). It never imports engine, db, llm or blocks.

## Processes and security

```
renderer (React, sandboxed)  ──api.x.y(…)──▶  preload (allow-list)  ──IPC──▶  main (Node)
   no Node, no fs, no network                                              engine · SQLite · LLM · files · keychain
           ◀──────────────── runs.onUpdate(run) push events ────────────────────────┘
```

- `contextIsolation`, `sandbox` and no `nodeIntegration`. Production builds get a strict CSP
  (`connect-src 'self'`): all network calls (Claude, web search) happen in main.
- The preload only forwards channels listed in `IPC_INVOKE_METHODS`. Main also checks that the sender is the app window.
- The window never navigates away. `http(s)` links open in the user's browser.
- API keys are entered in Settings, encrypted with Electron `safeStorage` (OS keychain) and never sent to
  the renderer. In dev, `apps/desktop/.env` is also read (see `.env.example`).

## The building blocks (`packages/core/src/blocks.ts`)

A workflow is a tree of **workplaces**. Each workplace holds blocks and edges. Seven kinds of block
are in the palette, defined once in `BLOCK_SPECS` (label, description, group, params, ports, whether
it has an inner workplace):

| Block       | Ports                                 | Inner workplace | Params (placeholders for now)                                                   |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Custom      | 1 in · 1 out                          | yes             | none                                                                            |
| Raw         | no input · 1 out (data stream)        | no              | Excel/CSV/SQLite or Research JSON import, dataset, file/query                   |
| Research    | no input · 1 out (same format as Raw) | yes             | question, source types, market, age, results                                    |
| AI Filter   | 1 in · 1 out (kept)                   | yes             | criterion, model, min. confidence                                               |
| AI Splitter | 1 in · 2–10 outputs                   | yes             | customer priority, car parts, custom or legacy routing, branches, model         |
| HIL         | 1 in · 1 out                          | no              | reviewer, instructions, approvals, edits                                        |
| Add to Car  | one in **per priority** + context ins | no              | priorities, contexts (Auto / Sales volumes), max. requirements, vehicle, market |

- **Ports** come from `blockPorts(block)`. They can depend on params (the splitter's `branches`, Add to
  Car's `priorities` → `in-0` "1. Priority" … and `contexts` → `ctx-0` "Context 1 · Auto" …), and port
  ids are positional (`out-0`, `in-2`, `ctx-0`). Older flows are migrated on load (`migrateGraph`). When params change, `setBlockParams`
  removes edges on ports that no longer exist and returns them, so the editor can tell the user.
- **Params** are declared as `ParamSpec`s (text, textarea, number, slider, select, multiselect, toggle,
  list — free text, or one of `itemOptions` per entry — and file). The editor renders a form from them, and `parseBlockParams` validates strictly (unknown
  keys and wrong types are errors). Select options with the value `"global"` mean "use Settings →
  Global parameters".
- **Inner workplaces** (Custom, Research, AI Filter) hold a sub-flow built from the same blocks,
  recursively. Each one has fixed **boundary blocks**: one `block_input` per input port of the parent
  and one `block_output` per output port. They are created with the block and can't be deleted.
- **Ids** are unique across the whole tree, so run status and outputs are keyed by block id alone.
- **Graph rules** live in `packages/core/src/graph.ts` and are shared by the editor and the engine:
  `checkConnection` (ports exist, no self-loop, no duplicates, no cycles), `connect`, `removeBlocks`,
  `setBlockParams`, `graphAt` / `updateGraphAt` (navigate the tree), `validateGraph` (everything,
  recursively). Several edges may enter one input (merged) or leave one output (fan-out).

## Add to Car agents

`packages/blocks/src/add-to-car/agents/`. Code does everything that must be exact; models read,
group, write and judge. One run of the block:

```
context reader ─┐ (sales volumes summarized by code; Auto: a data profile the reader explains)
analysts (map) ─┴→ synthesizer (themes) → code picks themes → architect ⇄ critic → judge → code
```

- **Analysts** read the priority inputs in batches (≤ 50 records, ≤ 14k chars, one input per batch)
  and return signals with record refs and quotes. Code checks every quote against the record
  (`findVerbatim`; a quote that isn't verbatim becomes the record's opening words) and turns signals
  into `Finding`s. Upstream findings are reused as they are.
- **Synthesizer** groups signals into themes (per category when there are many, then a merge pass).
  **Code** picks the themes: most important input first, then evidence weight (mentions ÷ rank);
  single comments and themes below `maxRequirements` are listed as held back, never dropped silently.
- **Architect** writes one requirement per theme from its strongest signals and the context briefs;
  the **critic** reviews it (accept / one rewrite / reject) and scores the six factors.
- **Judge** answers four typed questions (backed by evidence? customer-facing? still wanted at launch?
  testable?) through a `DecisionClient`: TypeSafe Jev (a "System 1" decision model with calibrated
  probabilities) or any LLM answering the same questions.
- **Code** assigns ids, priority from the input rank (first third of n inputs must, then should,
  then could), the critic's weighted score, evidence level A–D, and the confidence: a weighted
  geometric mean of the judge's answers, evidence breadth, the critic's verdict and conflicts.
- Everything is recorded in a `ReasoningTrace` (`packages/core/src/reasoning.ts`), stored by run and
  block (`reasoning_traces`) and shown in the thought-process view (block button, inspector, Car → Why?).
- Each role runs on an API setup (Settings → AI → Agents; `apps/desktop/src/main/agents.ts`). Providers
  live in `packages/llm`: Claude (adaptive thinking by effort, summarized thinking kept for the trace),
  OpenAI / Gemini / OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions, TypeSafe Jev, and the offline mock, which runs
  the same pipeline by rules and marks everything "[Offline]".
- `npm run eval:f70` runs the agents on BMW's F70 files with the user's setups and prints numbers only;
  the full output goes to `data/raw/eval/` (gitignored).

## Data flow: one envelope per port

Every port carries a `PipelineData` envelope (`sources, records, findings, themes, requirements`).
Raw and Research emit sources and records (the "unified data stream"). Raw accepts Excel, CSV,
read-only SQLite queries, and declared Research JSON envelopes. JSON import validates core schemas
and references but preserves the original objects, extensions, provenance and envelope metadata;
it rejects duplicate identities and dangling evidence rather than dropping them. Later blocks enrich the same
envelope: AI Filter keeps matching items (and extracts evidence-linked findings), AI Splitter routes
items to one branch each, HIL passes on what the reviewer approved, and Add to Car's agents turn what
arrives on its priority inputs into requirements (the input it arrives on sets the ranking; context
inputs are background only, see "Add to Car agents"). Several edges into one input are combined
with `mergePipelineData` (concatenate, de-duplicate by `id`, later edge wins).

```ts
defineBlock({
  kind: "ai_filter",
  async run(inputs, params, ctx) {
    const input = inputs.in; // one envelope per input port id
    /* ctx.llm, ctx.audit, ctx.log … */
    return { status: "ok", outputs: { out: kept } }; // one envelope per output port id
  },
});
```

## Engine semantics (WS1 implements, everyone relies on)

1. **Validate before running** with `validateGraph`, and check that every block kind (except
   Custom) has an implementation (`BlockRegistry.missing()`). If anything fails, the run fails before it
   starts, with per-block errors.
2. **Execute each workplace in topological order.** A block's input per port is the merge of what its
   incoming edges carry. Store each block's output per port and push `BlockRun` status, counts, logs,
   progress and any analytical splitter report snapshot via `runs.onUpdate`.
3. **Inner workplaces.** A block whose inner workplace contains blocks runs that sub-flow: each
   `block_input` emits what arrived on its parent port, and what reaches each `block_output` becomes
   the parent's output on that port. A Custom block always runs its sub-flow. Research and AI Filter run
   their built-in implementation while their inner workplace is empty.
4. **Failure.** A block that throws is marked `failed`, its downstream blocks `skipped`, and the run
   `failed`. Nothing is partially published.
5. **Pause / resume.** HIL returns `{ status: "paused" }` → the run is `waiting_for_review`.
   `runs.resume` reloads what the reviewer changed, re-invokes the block with `ctx.resumed = true`, and continues.
6. **Cancel.** The run's `AbortSignal` fires, and blocks must stop promptly.
7. **Audit.** The engine logs `run.*` events, blocks log what they create or change, and handlers log human actions.

## IPC API (`packages/core/src/ipc.ts`)

UI code calls `api.<namespace>.<method>(…)` from `@/lib/api`. Main implements `ReqflowHandlers`
(`apps/desktop/src/main/handlers.ts`). Failures arrive as `ReqflowError` with a `code`
(`invalid_input`, `not_found`, `not_implemented`, `internal`, …). Arguments must be plain data. Main
validates every argument with the Zod schemas, because the renderer counts as untrusted input.

| Method                                               | Purpose                                                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

## HIL review report

Double-clicking a HIL block (or its report icon) opens `components/dataflow/report/HilReport.tsx`:

- **Flow chart** from `traceLineage(root, path, blockId)` (`packages/core/src/lineage.ts`): every step
  data passes through on its way into the block. It leaves inner workplaces through their
  `block_input` and traces through the sub-flow of upstream blocks that have blocks inside.
- **Data at a step** (table icon on every step; the HIL itself = "data at this point"). Steps without
  inputs (Raw) show their **real data** via `blocks.preview`, and so does a HIL fed directly by them.
  After a run it shows `api.runs.blockOutput()` of the step (for the HIL: the merge of what its
  incoming edges carried). Otherwise it says nothing has arrived yet; there is no demo data.
- At run time the HIL block (`packages/blocks/src/hil/hil.ts`) pauses the run until the review is done
  and then passes the data on unchanged; edits go through the requirement API (audited).

## AI Splitter: raw analysis and review

The raw-data splitter uses a standalone Mastra `Agent` behind the existing injected `LlmClient`.
It receives the run's model configuration and secret-store API key; the Agent is not attached to a
Mastra instance, tools, storage, memory or tracing. Structured requests use strict Zod validation,
one generation step and no retries. Tests can inject the Agent factory, while production defaults
to the standalone implementation. Legacy `priority`, `category`, `sentiment` and `custom` routing
modes remain available alongside raw-data `customer_priority`, `car_parts` and `custom` analysis.

Raw analysis discovers candidate needs in batches of at most 20 records, consolidates them globally,
then assigns against the consolidated catalog. Car-part/custom modes create exactly the configured
2–10 global groups before assignment; customer-priority mode uses canonical needs and creates 2–10
demand bands. Oversized prompts fail explicitly rather than truncating evidence. Code verifies
complete item/need coverage and each cited source, record, locator and verbatim excerpt. The model
does not return scores, unit IDs, routes or human decisions.

Demand counts distinct expressed feedback units, not unique customers or population prevalence;
customer count is unknown. Explicit original/provider identities and reimport evidence can deduplicate
units, while distinct record/customer identities remain independent even if their text matches.
Sales, equipment and other context are not votes. Frequency is the share of supporting feedback units
relative to the highest-supporting global group and is weighted 70%; mean explicitly expressed
supporting impact is weighted 30%. An absent impact anchor is `NULL`, not zero; without available
impact or supporting feedback, the score is `NULL`. Opposing and unclear evidence remains visible,
and confidence is not demand. Output retains a versioned analytical report with score method, group
scores, item assignments, evidence, source matrix, limitations and human review history. The report
is stored with the `BlockRun` snapshot and rendered as score, evidence-balance and source-by-group
graphics with exact evidence drill-down.

At a paused eligible HIL, a reviewer may correct individual item routes with a required rationale.
Corrections update the run's routing report and audit history; computed scores and original evidence
remain unchanged. The review is available only while the upstream splitter is behind the current
paused HIL with reviewer edits enabled. It never edits or decides a requirement; requirement
approval, rejection or deferral remains a separate human action on the Car page.

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

# Reference palette

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic - **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and
re-run the validator. Nothing else changes.

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout - so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* ...only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:where(:not([data-theme="light"])) .viz-root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #ffffff;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #ffffff;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

Declare the dark values under both scopes as above - the media query covers
the OS setting; the `data-theme` scope covers the viewer's theme toggle,
which must win both ways (the `:not(...)` guard lets a light stamp beat
OS-dark; `:where()` keeps the media block below the toggle scope).

## Categorical palette

Both modes are selected. The dark column is the same eight hues stepped for the
dark surface, not a separate palette:

| Slot | Hue | Light | Dark |
|------|-----|-------|------|
| 1 | blue | `#2a78d6` | `#3987e5` |
| 2 | orange | `#eb6834` | `#d95926` |
| 3 | aqua | `#1baf7a` | `#199e70` |
| 4 | yellow | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 5 | magenta | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
| 6 | green | `#008300` | `#008300` |
| 7 | violet | `#4a3aa7` | `#9085e9` |
| 8 | red | `#e34948` | `#e66767` |

This order passes every hard gate in both modes on the default *adjacent*
pairlist (stacks, bars, lines): worst adjacent CVD Delta E 9.1 light / 8.4 dark
(OKLab ×100, >=8 target), worst adjacent normal-vision Delta E 19.6 light / 19.3
dark (>=15 floor). Under `--pairs all` (scatter, bubble, choropleth, small
multiples) the full eight cannot clear the floors - with all 28 pairs in
play no ordering can (the pairlist no longer depends on order), and
re-stepping is off the table by the documented-palette rule - so those
chart forms carry a series cap: **the first three slots validate all-pairs
in both modes** (worst pair CVD Delta E 9.2 light / 9.4 dark, normal-vision 24.0
light / 20.9 dark - clear of the CVD warn band). Past three, fold to "Other" or
facet: the fourth slot puts yellow and orange on screen
together, and that pair fails the all-pairs floors (normal-vision 13.7
light; CVD 4.8 dark). Three light-mode slots (magenta, yellow, aqua)
sit below 3:1 contrast on the light surface: the **relief rule** applies (ship
visible direct labels or the table view). The dark steps were chosen for the
dark band (OKLCH L ~ 0.48-0.67, >= 3:1 on the dark surface) and validated as a
set. (Ordering history: adopted July 2026 for its more harmonious opening -
the same eight hues and steps as its predecessor, re-ordered, zero hex
changes. The predecessor validated its first FOUR slots all-pairs, with its
dark run in the 6-8 CVD warn band, so secondary encoding was required there;
this order deliberately trades that fourth slot - yellow now sits beside orange -
for better-looking leading colors. Revisit the trade if yellow<->orange
confusion shows up in real charts with four or more series; undoing it is a
pure re-order.) When you swap in your own ramps, hold your palette to the full
gate.

The slot **ordering** is the CVD-safety mechanism, not cosmetic - candidate
orderings were enumerated and only those clearing every adjacent gate in both
modes kept (see `color-formula.md` § Themes); this default is one of the
passing orders, picked among them for its opening colors. When you swap in
your brand's hues, do the same: run the validator on candidate orderings and
choose only among the passing ones.

## Sequential hue

Default single hue: **blue**, light->dark. When two sequential contexts appear at
once, the second takes the next categorical slot's hue (orange), each as its own
one-hue ramp.

| step | hex | step | hex | step | hex | step | hex |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | `#cde2fb` | 250 | `#86b6ef` | 400 | `#3987e5` | 550 | `#1c5cab` |
| 150 | `#b7d3f6` | 300 | `#6da7ec` | 450 | `#2a78d6` | 600 | `#184f95` |
| 200 | `#9ec5f4` | 350 | `#5598e7` | 500 | `#256abf` | 650 | `#104281` |
| | | | | | | 700 | `#0d366b` |

The full 100->700 range is for **sequential** encoding (continuous magnitude -
heatmaps, choropleths) where the lightest step means "near zero" and is allowed
to recede toward the surface. For an **ordinal** ramp (discrete ordered marks -
funnel stages, tiers - validated with `--ordinal`), the step nearest the surface
must still clear 2:1: on light, start no lighter than **step 250** (`#86b6ef`,
